title: 3. Information Framing
use_cases: Implement when hiding critical information inside action-heavy sequences to prevent immediate detection
Configure when allowing readers to form incorrect logical conclusions based on juxtaposed facts
Use when restricting reader knowledge to a specific character's limited perspective
Implement when building long-term narrative payoffs through subtle foreshadowing
content:
This is a subtle but powerful trick. It’s how and when a clue is presented.

- Hiding Clues in Plain Sight: A vital piece of information is given during a tense, action-packed scene. Readers are so focused on the drama that they gloss over the important detail. Later, they realize they saw it but didn’t observe it.
- The Power of Assumption: The writer lets readers make a logical leap. For example: “He heard a gunshot and ran into the room. Mr. Smith was dead on the floor, a gun in his hand.” Many readers will assume suicide. But the text never says that. It just says the gun was in his hand. Who put it there?
- Selective Point of View: The story only shows us what one character sees and knows. If they don’t have all the information, neither do we. This naturally leads to misinterpretation.
